excerpt: Paano magtanim ng guyabano? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant guyabano (soursop), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: Young fruit trees planted in straight rows on cleared red soil

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant guyabano. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Filipino backyard growers and small farms raise guyabano from seed or a grafted seedling to the first fruit, the way most trees here are planted. It is a hardy lowland tree, so the guide keeps to the simple habits that work: a good hole, light feeding, a low shape, and bagging the fruit.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [guyabano nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/soursop-nutrient-deficiency). For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant guyabano

Seedlings are set out as the rains begin, about May to July, so they root before the dry months. Seeds are sown in the nursery about six months earlier. Trees flower and fruit on and off through the year, with most fruit in the rainy months.
What you plant

Most backyard trees come from seed of large, sweet, well shaped fruit. The seeds are washed clean of pulp, dried in the shade, and soaked in water overnight before sowing. They sprout in a few weeks. Growers who want early, true to type fruit buy grafted or marcotted seedlings of a known sweet or prolific type from a nursery.
Paano magtanim ng guyabano, step by step

Seedling trees usually give their first fruit in the third year after planting out, about 36 months (1,080 days). Grafted or marcotted trees often fruit a year earlier. The crop is ready about 3 years after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before planting: Dig the holes
items.text: Clear the spot and dig a hole about 30 to 50 cm wide and deep for each tree, in a sunny place where rain water does not stand. Mix the topsoil with a few kilos of rotted manure or compost and fill it back.

blocks.text: The nursery (Punlaan)

items.title: 6 months before planting: Sow the seeds in bags
items.text: Wash the seeds from a good fruit, dry them in the shade, and soak them overnight. Sow one or two seeds about 1 to 2 cm deep in each bag of garden soil mixed with compost, and keep the bags in light shade and moist.

items.title: 5 months before planting: Thin to one seedling
items.text: When the seedlings are up, keep the strongest one in each bag and pull out the rest. Water them every day or two and pull weeds from the bags.

items.title: 30 days before planting: Harden the seedlings
items.text: A month before planting, move the bags into fuller sun and water a little less so the leaves toughen. Seedlings about 30 to 50 cm tall are ready.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant at the start of the rains
items.text: On a cloudy day or late afternoon, water the bag, cut it away, and set the seedling in the hole at the same depth it grew. Firm the soil, water it, and tie it loosely to a stake if the place is windy. Tip: Keep a grafted seedling's graft joint above the soil.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 3: Mulch around the base
items.text: Spread dry grass, leaves or rice straw around the young tree, keeping it a hand's width from the stem, to hold moisture and keep the weeds down.

items.title: Day 30: Water in dry spells
items.text: Water young trees once or twice a week when the rain stops, through the first dry season. Older trees live on rain.

items.title: Month 2: Ring weed and feed
items.text: Keep a clean ring under the tree and give compost or manure, and a small handful of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) for those who use it, spread around the edge of the leaves. Feed at the start and the end of the rains, a little more each year.

items.title: Month 12: Shape a low tree
items.text: When the tree is about 1 m tall, cut the tip so it branches, and keep three or four strong branches spread out. Remove shoots below them and upright water sprouts, so the tree stays low and easy to pick.

items.title: Month 30: Help the flowers set
items.text: Flowers come on the trunk and older branches. Some growers dust pollen from an open flower into others with a soft brush in the morning, because poorly pollinated fruit grows crooked and small.

items.title: Month 31: Bag the young fruit
items.text: When the fruit is small, about the size of an egg, wrap it in a net, paper or plastic bag open at the bottom to keep fruit borers and fruit flies out. Remove fruit that is badly misshapen or bored.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 3: Pick mature fruit
items.text: The first fruit usually comes in the third year. Pick when the skin turns from dark, shiny green to a dull yellowish green and the soft spines spread apart. Cut the stalk and catch the fruit so it does not drop. Tip: Let it soften on a table for a few days before eating.

items.title: Month 37: Prune after fruiting
items.text: After the main crop, cut out dead, crossing and crowded branches and any water sprouts, and give the tree compost or manure to build the next crop.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for guyabano
Spacing
About 4 to 6 m between trees each way in an orchard. Backyard trees are planted alone, a few meters from the house or fence. One seedling a hole.
Water
Rain fed in most farms. Young trees are watered once or twice a week in their first dry season. Older trees get water only in long droughts. The tree does not like standing water.
Fertilizer

Rotted manure, compost and kitchen ash around the tree, at planting and each year at the start of the rains. Farmers who buy fertilizer give complete fertilizer (14 14 14) twice a year, a small handful for young trees and more as the tree grows. Many backyard trees get nothing and still bear, but smaller crops. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Ring weeding and mulch, watering young trees in the dry season, cutting the tip to make a low tree with three or four main branches, removing water sprouts, pruning after the crop, hand pollinating in the morning, and bagging young fruit against borers.
When and how to harvest

Fruit is mature when the skin turns from dark shiny green to dull yellowish green and the spines soften and spread apart. It is picked firm and ripened indoors in a few days, because a soft ripe fruit bruises and splits if it falls. Ripe fruit spoils fast, so it is sold or eaten quickly.
Common mistakes when planting guyabano

items: Planting in a low spot where water stands after rain.
Sowing seeds from small or poorly shaped fruit.
Letting the tree grow tall with no pruning, so the fruit is out of reach.
Leaving young fruit unbagged, so borers and fruit flies spoil most of it.
Waiting for the fruit to soften on the tree, so it falls and bursts.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of guyabano
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Plant grafted or marcotted seedlings of a known sweet, prolific type for earlier, even fruit.
Test the soil and feed by the result, twice a year, more as the tree grows.
Hand pollinate in the morning to get round, full fruit.
Bag every young fruit and pick up fallen and bored fruit to break the pest cycle.
Prune every year after fruiting to keep the tree low and open, and use integrated pest management.
